questions.q: What is a 'go/no-go checkpoint' as used in this capstone?
options: An automatic transition between chapters with no decision involved
A deliberate pause between project phases where continuing is explicitly justified by the evidence, not assumed
A quiz students must pass before unlocking the next chapter
A performance benchmark for the C++ code
questions.explain: A go/no-go checkpoint is a deliberate decision point between phases where the team explicitly decides, based on evidence, whether to proceed — not an assumption that work automatically continues.

questions.q: What was the checkpoint decision at the end of Phase 1, and why?
options: No-go, because the effect was not statistically significant anywhere
Go, because the evidence supports a real, modest reversal effect that strengthens in high-VIX regimes exactly as the hypothesis predicted
Go, because any statistically significant number justifies proceeding regardless of context
No-go, because the data could not be cleaned properly
questions.explain: The decision was go: the evidence shows a real, if modest, reversal effect that strengthens specifically in high-VIX regimes, matching the original hypothesis — a more convincing pattern than an isolated significant number.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what would the honest response have been if the statistics had come back null?
options: Quietly re-run tests on different data cuts until something looked significant
Narrow the hypothesis and retest, report the null result plainly, or stop the project at Phase 1
Proceed to build the model and backtest anyway, since effort was already invested
Redefine the success criteria after the fact to match whatever was found
questions.explain: A rigorous process responds to a null result by narrowing the hypothesis and retesting, reporting the null honestly, or stopping — not by chasing significance or redefining success after seeing the data.

questions.q: Why does this lesson emphasize that success criteria were set in Lesson 3, before the statistical tests ran?
options: Because it made the C++ code run faster
Because preregistering criteria before seeing results prevents quietly redefining success to fit whatever the data happened to show
Because Lesson 3 is a legal requirement for publishing research
Because it determines which ETFs are included in the universe
questions.explain: Preregistration (from Lesson 3) means success/failure was defined before any results existed, so the checkpoint decision couldn't be rationalized after the fact.

questions.q: Which piece of evidence most directly supports proceeding to Phase 2 rather than just a single significant t-stat?
options: The fact that SPY data was available from Stooq
The fact that the reversal effect is concentrated in high-VIX regimes, matching the economic story the hypothesis predicted, rather than appearing as an isolated, unexplained number
The fact that XLC and XLRE launched partway through the sample
The fact that the C++ core computes rolling z-scores quickly
questions.explain: The VIX-regime dependence matching the original economic hypothesis (overreaction during fear, not calm) is more convincing than an isolated significant statistic, because it's consistent with a plausible underlying mechanism.
